newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Kremlin tries to pour oil over troubled waters.
newsitem.headline: Kremlin tries to pour oil over troubled waters.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin and senior Kremlin officials are doing their best to restore some sense of order to Russian politics after the turmoil caused by the sacking on Thursday of outspoken security chief Alexander Lebed.
On Saturday Yeltsin replaced Lebed with quiet-spoken former parliamentary speaker Ivan Rybkin, a man who can be relied upon to obey orders and not rock the boat.
"I am sure you will succeed," Yeltsin told Rybkin in brief televised comments. "Good luck."

Rybkin, appointed to the posts of secretary to the Security Council and Yeltsin envoy to Chechnya, said he would continue Lebed's efforts to bring peace to the breakaway region "but in a businesslike manner, without fuss and noise".

Lebed responded in kind, dismissing Rybkin, a former communist who did his best to prevent parliament clashing with Yeltsin during his two years in power, as an incompetent lightweight bureaucrat who was doomed to failure.

Chechen separatists, who took the explosive Lebed to their hearts, say his dismissal could lead to a deterioration of the situation there. They might also start worrying that Rybkin could be pushed aside by hardliners keen to restart the war.

But whatever his faults, Rybkin is likely to be welcomed with relief in Kremlin corridors still reverberating from the after-effects of Lebed's tumultuous four months in power during which he alienated foe and friend alike.
The former paratroop general, widely popular among the armed forces rank and file, raised hackles by predicting shortages of cash in the military would lead to a "hot autumn".
In reply, Defence Minister Igor Rodionov chided unnamed politicians whose "careless acts...cause colossal damage".

"The situation in the armed forces is rather complicated, first of all because of lack of normal financing. But regardless of this, the situation is fully under control and manageable," Rodionov told Russian television on Saturday.
Lebed is out in the cold, for the time being at least. If he is to realise his dream of becoming president he may need to gather a team with more political skill than he has demonstrated so far.
Former Soviet president Mikhail Gorbachev said Lebed could become one of the leading contenders in a future presidential election as long he created a powerful democratic movement to support him.

"Lebed came to power with the goal of changing policies, ending the war in Chechnya, and striking a blow against corrpution and crime (but) he wasn't allowed to do anything," Gorbachev told Interfax news agency.

"But (he) allowed people a glance into what could be seen in the corridors of power: chaos, panic and people without any ideas as to what to do," said Gorbachev, calling once again on his old foe Yeltsin to resign.
